covered: Latitude and longitude as angular coordinates, with the crucial asymmetry that latitude has a natural zero and longitude does not.
Parallels versus meridians, and the variation in the length of a degree of longitude from about 111 km at the Equator to about 56 km at 60°N.
Great circles and small circles, with the Equator as the only great-circle parallel.
The five major circles (Equator, tropics at 23½°, polar circles at 66½°) derived from the Earth's axial tilt, and their consequences for insolation, climate belts, Coriolis strength and day length.
Longitude as time: 15° = 1 hour, 1° = 4 minutes, 1′ of arc = 4 seconds, with Delhi's ~21-minute local lag behind IST as the worked Indian example.
Local versus standard time, the 1884 International Meridian Conference and the choice of Greenwich, and why time-zone boundaries are political rather than geometric.
India's standard meridian at 82°30′E (UTC+5:30), the arithmetic behind the half-hour offset, and the two-time-zone debate.
The International Date Line: its zig-zag, the Kiribati (1995) and Samoa (2011) adjustments, and the westward-add / eastward-subtract rule.
lastHandoff.next: Lesson 3: Reading the Earth — Maps, Scale and Projections. Map scale in statement, representative fraction and graphical forms; large versus small-scale maps; the necessity of distortion; Mercator, conic and azimuthal projections; topographic sheets, contours and conventional signs; remote sensing and GIS; and the closing argument that every map is an argument.
lastHandoff.notes: The Eratosthenes callback was reused deliberately in the opening of Section 1 (reference frames) and again in Section 3 (measuring an arc on a sphere; the longitude problem and Harrison's chronometers). Do not re-explain the oblate spheroid or the solar-system material. The Delhi–New York great-circle image was carried forward in Section 1 as a bridge to the projection lesson — pick it up again in Lesson 3 when discussing why Mercator's straight lines were a navigational triumph and a cartographic distortion. Figure 'latitude-belts' is reusable whenever climate belts, insolation angles or day length come up (monsoon, pressure belts, biomes). Figure 'time-strip' is reusable in the context of globalisation, markets and geopolitics. Figure 'india-meridian' is reusable in the two-time-zone debate and in any discussion of India's physiographic extent. The 'map as argument' stance from Lesson 1 was restated at the end of Section 5 and should be the hinge into Lesson 3.
